neighbors.heading: ask God to choose
neighbors.text: Today Ignatius asked for a level scale before a big choice. The Qur'an says: "it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you, and it may happen that ye love a thing which is bad for you. Allah knoweth, ye know not." Before a decision, Muslims may pray istikhara: if this is good for me, make it easy; if not, turn it away.
neighbors.difference: Ignatius asks the chooser to weigh, sift the heart's movements and then choose, often with a director's help. In istikhara, a Muslim prays and hands the outcome to God, then reads what unfolds. Both still act; the weight falls differently.
neighbors.shared: you can want something badly and still hold it open.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:216 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, the istikhara prayer, narrated by Jabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what's up to you
neighbors.text: Today Ignatius drew a line: weigh only where the choice is free. A Stoic teacher who had once been enslaved, Epictetus, drew a line like it. The handbook of his teaching opens: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Your body, your reputation, what others think: not fully yours. Your judgments and choices: yours. Peace, he taught, starts on the right side of that line.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus seeks calm through reason: care only about your own choices. Ignatius isn't after calm for its own sake; indifference keeps the heart free so it can choose what leads to God and love the people in front of it.
neighbors.shared: some things are yours to choose, and some you can hold lightly.
neighbors.sources: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (Long 1877)

neighbors.heading: sweetness and humility
neighbors.text: Today Ignatius traced pride's slow road: a little more, then being noticed, then pride. The Sikh Gurus name that pull haumai, ego, the voice that says I, me, mine. Ego is a deep, lasting illness, Guru Angad says, and its cure lies within it too. Guru Nanak gives the medicine in one line: sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtues.
neighbors.difference: Ignatius pictures two leaders, Christ and the enemy of our nature, calling people to two banners. Sikh teaching places the struggle inside, between ego and the remembered Name, with the Guru's word as the way out.
neighbors.shared: humility is a small first step that opens every other door.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466 (Guru Angad, Asa di Var) (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470 (Guru Nanak, Asa di Var) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two kinds of wealth
neighbors.text: Today Ignatius set two banners on two fields. The Bhagavad Gita draws its own line and calls the two sides two kinds of wealth. Krishna lists the qualities that free a person: fearlessness, honesty, gentleness, no excess pride. Then the ones that bind: showiness, arrogance, anger, harshness, and the restless thought, this I gained today, that I'll get tomorrow.
neighbors.difference: For Ignatius the choice is a call to follow Christ, who chose to be poor and humble. In the Gita the freeing qualities are a nature to grow into, leading the self toward liberation; the binding ones keep it circling.
neighbors.shared: what you chase quietly shapes who you become.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 16.1–5, 16.13 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when walking, know you're walking
neighbors.text: Today the early Jesuits carried prayer into the classroom and onto the road. The Buddha taught a carried attention too. In his talk on the foundations of mindfulness, he says that when walking, a practitioner knows they are walking; when eating, drinking, bending or stretching, they act with clear awareness. Not only on the cushion: in every ordinary motion of the day.
neighbors.difference: The Jesuits carry an awareness of God, present and at work in all things. Buddhist mindfulness doesn't turn toward a creator; it trains clear seeing of body, feeling and mind as they arise and pass.
neighbors.shared: a busy day can still have a quiet center.
neighbors.sources: Satipatthana Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 10 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who sweeps a room
neighbors.text: Today the Jesuits said the sickroom and the road are where prayer goes. An Anglican parish priest, George Herbert, put that in a poem now sung as a hymn. Ordinary work done for God, he wrote, turns to gold: "A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine: / Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine."
neighbors.difference: Ignatius built this into a religious order, with vows, the Exercises and a daily examen. Herbert, a married country priest, handed it to anyone holding a broom, with no order or rule attached.
neighbors.shared: ordinary work, done with love, can become a prayer.
neighbors.sources: George Herbert, "The Elixir," The Temple (1633) · 1 Thessalonians 5:17

neighbors.heading: a back room of your own
neighbors.text: Today the Carmelite hermits were told to stay in their cells. A French essayist, Michel de Montaigne, gave people with busy houses similar advice. Keep a back room of your own, he wrote, wholly free, where you can retreat and talk with yourself, so that if family or fortune is lost, something steady remains.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne's back room is for freedom and knowing yourself, a place to keep your footing. The Carmelite cell is for prayer: keeping watch with God under a rule, and coming back to it again and again.
neighbors.shared: everyone needs a small room to come back to.
neighbors.sources: Michel de Montaigne, Essays I.39, "Of Solitude" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: day and night
neighbors.text: Today the Rule of Carmel borrowed a line from Psalm one. That psalm was Jewish first: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in His law doth he meditate day and night." Jewish tradition took it into the study house, where people return to Torah again and again. The sages put it simply: make your Torah study a fixed habit.
neighbors.difference: The Carmelite meditates alone in a cell and reads the law of the Lord in the light of Christ. Jewish study is often out loud, with a partner, arguing over the text, and the law is the Torah itself, lived as commandments.
neighbors.shared: the words you return to every day become your home.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 1:2 (JPS 1917) · Pirkei Avot 1:15 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: my devotee and my friend
neighbors.text: Today Teresa called prayer a friendly conversation with the one who loves us. The Bhagavad Gita is itself a talk between friends, on a chariot before a battle. Krishna tells Arjuna why he's sharing this ancient teaching with him: you are my devotee and my friend. Later, Arjuna remembers joking with him, eating and resting beside him, never guessing who his friend was.
neighbors.difference: Teresa's friend is Jesus, who Christians believe became human once, for good. For many Hindus, Krishna is God himself, who says in the Gita that he comes age after age to protect the good.
neighbors.shared: the one you pray to can also be a friend.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 4.3; 11.41–42 (paraphrase) · Bhagavad Gita 4.7–8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I am near
neighbors.text: Today Teresa said the friendship starts from God's side. The Qur'an speaks of that closeness directly: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me." Alongside the five daily prayers, Muslims make du'a: personal prayer in their own words, any time, about anything.
neighbors.difference: Teresa's friend is Jesus, God made man. In Islam God is near yet like nothing he made; Muslims call him al-Wadud, the Loving, and al-Wali, the protecting friend, and never one who took flesh.
neighbors.shared: you can speak to God about anything, in your own words.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:186 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 2:257 and 85:14, al-Wali and al-Wadud (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the church in their house
neighbors.text: Today Secular Carmelites carried prayer home to jobs, kids and bills. The first Christians often met in homes. Paul ends a letter greeting a married couple, Priscilla and Aquila, and adds: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house." Protestant family devotions keep that habit alive: a Bible and a prayer at the kitchen table, with a parent leading.
neighbors.difference: Secular Carmelites make a promise and belong to an order, with a rule of daily mental prayer. In much of Protestant life there are no lay orders; the home itself, with the Bible and family prayer, is where everyday faith is kept.
neighbors.shared: a kitchen can be a holy place.
neighbors.sources: Romans 16:5 (KJV) · Protestant family devotions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: laughing, playing, eating
neighbors.text: Today Carmel's desert fit into a kitchen. Sikh teaching keeps the holy in the kitchen. The Gurus turned away from leaving home to find God; they married, farmed and worked, and taught the householder's path. Guru Arjan sings that, meeting the true Guru, a person finds the way, and while laughing, playing, dressing and eating, is set free.
neighbors.difference: Secular Carmelites are laypeople joined to an order whose friars and nuns live in monasteries. Sikh teaching sets aside monastic withdrawal; Sikhs are called to the householder's life of prayer, honest work and sharing.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to leave home to find what's holy.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522 (Guru Arjan, Gujri ki Var) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a whole world
neighbors.text: Today Genesis said every person bears God's image. The rabbis drew a picture from that. God made one Adam first, the Mishnah says, so whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one, a whole world. A king stamps coins from one seal and they all look alike; God stamps everyone from Adam's seal, and no two are alike.
neighbors.difference: Catholics read the image of God through Jesus, who says what's done to the least is done to him. Jewish teaching reads it from Adam and the Torah, without Christ, and carries each life's worth into daily law.
neighbors.shared: no one is extra; each person is a whole world.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 1:27 · Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the turtle and the yoke
neighbors.text: Today the lesson said dignity comes with being human. The Buddha told a story about how rare that is. Picture a yoke with one hole, tossed on the ocean, and a blind turtle that rises once in a hundred years. The chance its head goes through the hole, he said, is better than the chance of a human birth. A human life is a rare chance to wake up.
neighbors.difference: Catholics ground dignity in a Creator who made each person in his image. Buddhists see a human life as precious for its rare chance to awaken, with no creator behind it, and extend that care to every living being.
neighbors.shared: your life is rare; so is the one beside you.
neighbors.sources: Samyutta Nikaya 56.47–48 (paraphrase) · Balapandita Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 129 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one body, one fever
neighbors.text: Today Paul said when one member suffers, all suffer. The Prophet Muhammad used the same picture. The believers, in their love, mercy and kindness to one another, are like one body, he said: when one limb aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. And the Qur'an widens the circle: all people were created from a single soul.
neighbors.difference: The hadith speaks first of the community of believers; the Qur'an grounds the wider human family in one soul. Paul's body is the Church in Christ, and Catholic teaching stretches solidarity to every person, whatever their religion.
neighbors.shared: when one of us hurts, the rest can't sleep easy.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the believers as one body (paraphrase) · Qur'an 4:1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the swarm and the bee
neighbors.text: Today solidarity meant everyone is responsible for everyone. A Roman emperor wrote something close in his private notebook. Marcus Aurelius reminded himself that people are made to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids. And in one short line: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee."
neighbors.difference: Marcus grounds it in a shared human reason and nature, not a personal God or a church. Catholic solidarity rests on one Creator who made all people one family, and on Christ, who bears our burdens.
neighbors.shared: what's good for all of us is good for each of us.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.54 (Long 1862) · Meditations 2.1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Lalo's bread
neighbors.text: Today a pope said work is for the person, not the person for work. Sikhs tell a story about that. Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a poor carpenter, and turned down a feast from Malik Bhago, a rich official. Tradition says he squeezed the two breads: from Lalo's honest bread came milk; from the bread made of others' stolen labor came blood.
neighbors.difference: Laborem Exercens adds the cross: hard work, borne patiently, as a share in Christ's suffering. Sikh teaching joins honest work to remembering God's Name and sharing with others, without that picture of the cross.
neighbors.shared: bread earned honestly feeds more than the body.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: blessing the tools
neighbors.text: Today the lesson said machines are earlier human work, piled up. Some Hindus honor the maker in the tools. The Rig Veda praises Vishvakarman, the All-Maker, who shaped heaven and earth. On Vishwakarma Puja, workers in parts of India clean their machines and tools, garland them, and set them down for the day, giving thanks for the craft that feeds their families.
neighbors.difference: On Vishwakarma Puja, tools are honored as gifts of the divine maker. Laborem Exercens honors tools too, as the fruit of earlier work, but keeps one order clear: things serve persons, and the worker comes first.
neighbors.shared: the hands that make things deserve honor, and rest.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 10.81–82, hymns to Vishvakarman (paraphrase) · Vishwakarma Puja in Hindu practice (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when this is, that is
neighbors.text: Today Francis said everything is connected. The Buddha put a version of that at the heart of his teaching: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises; when this is not, that is not. Nothing stands alone. A meal, a forest, a mood all depend on countless conditions, and they change when those conditions change.
neighbors.difference: Francis's web starts in God's delight: a world made and called very good. Buddhist dependent arising describes how things come to be without a creator behind them, and uses that insight to loosen craving and suffering.
neighbors.shared: nothing you do touches only you.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 38 and 79 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: to dress it and to keep it
neighbors.text: Today Francis wrote to everyone about our common home. Other Christians read the same Bible toward the same care. Genesis says God put the first human in the garden "to dress it and to keep it." Protestant churches speak of creation care, and the Orthodox Patriarch Bartholomew, whom Francis quotes, calls harming the natural world a sin against ourselves and God.
neighbors.difference: Laudato Si' is one teaching letter from a pope, addressed to the whole Church and beyond. Protestant and Orthodox Christians have no pope; their creation care grows in each church's own voice, from patriarchs and synods to local congregations.
neighbors.shared: the earth is a gift to tend, not a thing to use up.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 2:15 (KJV) · Patriarch Bartholomew, quoted in Laudato Si' 8–9 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: enough, and as good
neighbors.text: Today the lesson asked of what you own: what is this for? An English philosopher, John Locke, wrote a classic defense of owning things: mix your labor into something and it becomes yours. But he set a limit. It holds "at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others." And no one may take more than they can use before it spoils.
neighbors.difference: Locke also begins with the earth given in common, then builds strong rights from labor. Catholic teaching keeps the gift in front: owning is a stewardship, and every possession is still asked what it is for.
neighbors.shared: having enough means leaving enough for someone else.
neighbors.sources: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), §27 · §31 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the corner of the field
neighbors.text: Today the Catechism said the earth's goods are meant for everyone. The Torah writes that into the harvest. When you reap, Leviticus says, don't reap the corners of your field or gather what falls; leave them for the poor and the stranger. And the psalm the lesson quoted was Jewish first: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof."
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching states a principle and leaves its shape to conscience and society. Jewish law spells out duties: a corner left standing, the gleanings, a tithe for the poor, with detailed rules the rabbis worked out in a whole Mishnah tractate.
neighbors.shared: some of every harvest already belongs to someone else.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:9–10 (paraphrase) · Psalm 24:1 (JPS 1917) · Mishnah, tractate Peah (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the king who gave his last cup
neighbors.text: Today Dorothy Day showed mercy that costs. The Bhagavata Purana tells of King Rantideva, who gave away everything and went hungry for many days. When food and water finally came, guests kept arriving: a priest, a laborer, a man with his dogs, an outcast. He gave it all away. He wanted no reward, he prayed, only to take on the suffering of every being.
neighbors.difference: Day met Christ in the poor, because Jesus says what's done to the least is done to him. Rantideva sees God dwelling in every being, people and animals alike, and serves each one as God's own home.
neighbors.shared: real mercy often costs something, and gives more back.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana 9.21 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: though they loved it themselves
neighbors.text: Today Day's mercy cost her sleep, comfort and money. The Qur'an praises giving that costs. The righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, it says, though they love that food themselves, and tell them: we feed you only for God's sake; we want no reward or thanks from you. The phrase can also be read: for love of Him.
neighbors.difference: Day lived among the poor in houses of hospitality and saw Christ in each guest. In Islam, giving is woven into worship itself, from freely given charity to zakat, a set share of wealth owed to those in need.
neighbors.shared: give the bread you wanted, and wish for no thanks.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 76:8–9 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:177 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: good Lord, deliver us
neighbors.text: Today the litany called out name after name, and the people answered. Anglicans pray a litany too, in the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. A leader prays through dangers and needs, from lightning and tempest to hardness of heart, and after each set the people answer: "Good Lord, deliver us." Later the answer changes: "We beseech thee to hear us, good Lord."
neighbors.difference: The Litany of Loreto turns to Mary and asks, pray for us. The Prayer Book litany addresses God alone; the old lines asking saints to pray were taken out, a choice that marks a real difference between the two churches.
neighbors.shared: a long prayer said together carries the ones too tired to pray.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer (1662), The Litany

neighbors.heading: a litany of names
neighbors.text: Today the Litany of Loreto called Mary by many names, because one name never covers anyone you love. Sikhs pray a long chant of names too: Jaap Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, part of the daily morning prayers. Line after line salutes God: to the Timeless, salutation; to the Merciful, salutation; to the One without form, salutation; to the One beyond all names.
neighbors.difference: Loreto's names belong to Mary, a human mother whom Catholics ask to pray for them. Jaap Sahib's names all belong to the one formless God, who Sikhs believe is never born and never takes a body.
neighbors.shared: love keeps reaching for one more name.
neighbors.sources: Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh, Dasam Granth (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: it is not in heaven
neighbors.text: Today the Church said no vision, even an approved one, adds to the faith. The rabbis tell a bold story. In a dispute over an oven, a voice from heaven took Rabbi Eliezer's side. Rabbi Joshua stood and quoted the Torah: "It is not in heaven." The Torah was given at Sinai, the sages said; now it is read and decided here, by people.
neighbors.difference: Catholics hold that God said everything in Christ, and the Church judges reported visions. For the rabbis, the Torah given at Sinai is the root, and the sages decide its meaning by reasoning together, even against a heavenly voice.
neighbors.shared: a wonder is welcome, but the old words stay the anchor.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 30:12 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the wonder of teaching
neighbors.text: Today the Church said approved apparitions are never required belief. The Buddha was wary of wonders too. In one discourse, a man asks him to have a monk work a miracle so more people will believe. The Buddha says he dislikes such wonders, since doubters can explain them away. The wonder he praises is instruction: teaching that changes how a person lives.
neighbors.difference: Catholics believe God can work real miracles, and some apparitions are approved to be honored. The Buddha doesn't deny unusual powers but sets them aside; what matters is a teaching each person can practice and see for themselves.
neighbors.shared: the truest sign is a life that changes.
neighbors.sources: Kevaddha Sutta, Digha Nikaya 11 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a spring in the valley
neighbors.text: Today a girl dug in the mud at Lourdes, and water came. Muslims tell of another spring. Hajar, alone in a dry valley with her baby Ismail, ran between two hills looking for water. An angel struck the ground and water rose: Zamzam. Pilgrims to Mecca still walk her path between the hills, and drink from that well.
neighbors.difference: At Lourdes, Catholics honor a spring tied to Mary's appearing, which no Catholic is required to believe. Zamzam is tied to Hajar and Ismail, and walking her path is part of the pilgrimage rites themselves.
neighbors.shared: God can open water where there was only dust.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hajar and the well of Zamzam, narrated by Ibn Abbas (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:158 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: proportion your belief
neighbors.text: Today Lourdes sent claimed cures to doctors before anyone said miracle. A Scottish philosopher would have liked that step. David Hume wrote: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence." He doubted any report could prove a miracle. Someone on their own path can keep his rule and still honor a place where the sick go first.
neighbors.difference: Hume doubted that any testimony could ever establish a miracle. The Church holds that miracles can happen, examines claims slowly, approves few, and never requires a Catholic to believe in any particular cure at Lourdes.
neighbors.shared: hope doesn't have to be afraid of an honest question.
neighbors.sources: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), section X, "Of Miracles"

neighbors.heading: the whole sky as a plate
neighbors.text: Today children crowned Mary with flowers from the backyard. Tradition says Guru Nanak once watched a temple ceremony of lamps on a tray, and sang a different one. The sky is the plate, he sang, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls; the scented breeze is the incense, and all the forest's flowers are the offering.
neighbors.difference: Catholics crown a statue of Mary, honoring her as queen and mother, while keeping worship for God alone. Sikhs make no images and offer no flowers to them; Nanak's song turns the whole universe into praise of the formless One.
neighbors.shared: a flower given with love is never too small.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 663 (Guru Nanak, Raag Dhanasari) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today a child carried flowers to Mary, and the gift didn't have to last. Hindus know that kind of gift. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, I accept it, offered from a devoted heart. Fresh flowers at a home shrine are a daily offering in Hindu worship.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu worship, flowers are offered to God, often before a sacred image, in the form a family worships. Catholics crown Mary as queen because her son is king; she is honored and loved, and worship belongs to God alone.
neighbors.shared: love counts more than the size of the gift.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a sister, a wife
neighbors.text: Today the lesson met Peter's mother-in-law and a priest's wife at the coffee urn. Protestant churches made married clergy their ordinary way. Paul asks: "Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles?" Martin Luther, once a monk, married Katharina von Bora, and the pastor's household became part of Protestant life.
neighbors.difference: Eastern Catholic and Orthodox priests marry first and then may be ordained, and bishops stay celibate. Protestant churches don't require celibacy of their ministers, who may marry before or after ordination.
neighbors.shared: a family can carry a calling together.
neighbors.sources: 1 Corinthians 9:5 (KJV) · Augsburg Confession, article 23, on the marriage of priests (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the temple family
neighbors.text: Today the lesson met priests' wives and the respectful names they're given. Buddhism has both shapes too. Monks who keep the ancient monastic code leave marriage behind. But in Japan, the teacher Shinran openly married, and in the Pure Land school that follows him, temple priests marry and a family often keeps the temple from one generation to the next.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, priesthood is a sacrament, and marriage is a holy calling of its own. Shinran called himself neither monk nor layman, and his tradition remembers his marriage as a sign that the Buddha's compassion reaches householders just as they are.
neighbors.shared: holiness can live in a house with a family in it.
neighbors.sources: Shinran and the Jodo Shinshu tradition (paraphrase) · the Vinaya, the monastic code (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: becoming like God
neighbors.text: Today the Church spoke of sharing God's life, like iron glowing in a fire. A Greek philosopher reached for something close long before. In Plato's Theaetetus, Socrates says the way out of the world's troubles is to become like God as far as a person can, and that becoming like God means becoming just and holy, with wisdom.
neighbors.difference: Plato's likeness to God is a philosopher's climb, through wisdom and justice. Theosis is a gift: God became human to draw people into his life by grace, and they remain creatures, sharing the fire without becoming it.
neighbors.shared: you're made to grow toward the good, not stay where you are.
neighbors.sources: Plato, Theaetetus 176a–b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walk in His ways
neighbors.text: Today theosis said people are drawn into God's life. Jewish teaching speaks of walking in God's ways. "Ye shall be holy; for I the LORD your God am holy," Leviticus says. The Talmud asks how a person can walk after God, and answers: follow his deeds. As God clothed the naked, visited the sick, comforted mourners and buried the dead, so should you.
neighbors.difference: Catholics speak of sharing in God's own life through Christ, while remaining creatures. The Talmud speaks of imitating God's ways, kindness for kindness; the line between Creator and creature stays bright.
neighbors.shared: you become what you practice, kindness by kindness.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:2 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Sotah 14a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nine nights
neighbors.text: Today a novena kept nine days of prayer, one after another. Hindus keep nine too. Navaratri means nine nights, and many Hindus spend them honoring the Goddess, Durga and her forms, with fasting, lamps, songs and dance. The Devi Mahatmya, often recited in these days, tells how the Goddess rose to defeat a demon no one else could.
neighbors.difference: Navaratri is a festival at set times of year, with community celebrations, honoring the divine as Mother. A novena can start any week, for any need, and is prayed to God, often asking a saint to pray alongside.
neighbors.shared: keeping at it, night after night, is part of the prayer.
neighbors.sources: Devi Mahatmya (paraphrase) · Navaratri in Hindu practice (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the last ten nights
neighbors.text: Today the apostles waited nine days for a promise. Muslims keep their own nights of waiting. In the last ten nights of Ramadan, the Prophet Muhammad would stay in the mosque in prayer, and many Muslims still do. Among those nights is the Night of Power: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Its exact night isn't fixed, so they keep watch on many.
neighbors.difference: A novena is chosen by the one who prays, for a feast or an intention. Ramadan's last ten nights come once a year for the whole community, seeking the night when, Muslims believe, the Qur'an began to come down.
neighbors.shared: some prayers are about staying, night after night.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 97:3 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet's i'tikaf in the last ten days, narrated by Aisha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the pilgrim's progress
neighbors.text: Today the road itself became a prayer. John Bunyan, a Puritan preacher, turned the whole Christian life into one long pilgrimage. In The Pilgrim's Progress, a man called Christian leaves his city with a burden on his back. He trudges through the Slough of Despond, and at the cross the burden falls away. He keeps walking, through Vanity Fair, toward the Celestial City.
neighbors.difference: Catholic pilgrims travel to real shrines, holy places where prayer is made with the feet. Protestant reformers set shrine pilgrimages aside, and kept the road as a picture of the whole of life, walked anywhere.
neighbors.shared: life is a road, and you're not home yet.
neighbors.sources: John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress (1678) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the pilgrimage inside
neighbors.text: Today the Catechism called pilgrimage a picture of life's journey. Sikhs travel too, to Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where pilgrims bathe in its pool and eat together in the free kitchen. Yet Guru Nanak warned against trusting the trip alone. In Japji he sings: I would bathe at holy places if it pleased God; without that, what use is the bath?
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the journey to a holy place is itself a prayer and a time of renewal. Sikh teaching honors historic gurdwaras but holds that travel and bathing don't wash the heart; remembering God's Name does.
neighbors.shared: the road matters most when the heart walks it too.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 6, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: eat, be full, bless
neighbors.text: Today grace called dinner a gift before anything else. Jewish blessings over food go back to the Torah: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." And before bread, Jews say a short blessing praising God, who brings forth bread from the earth.
neighbors.difference: Catholic grace is mostly said before the meal and goes through Christ. In Jewish law, the Torah's command is the blessing after eating, the longer grace called Birkat Hamazon, with different short blessings before bread, fruit and wine.
neighbors.shared: the food was a gift; saying so changes the meal.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 8:10 (KJV) · the blessing over bread, Talmud, Berakhot 38a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not for fun, not for show
neighbors.text: Today the table grace slowed the meal down. Buddhist monks have their own pause. The Buddha taught them to reflect before eating: this food is not for fun, not for pride, not for looks, but to keep this body going, to ease hunger and to support the practice. In many monasteries the reflection is chanted together before the meal.
neighbors.difference: Catholic grace thanks God as the giver, through Christ. The Buddhist reflection isn't thanks to a creator; it is wise attention to why you eat, and to the people whose gifts filled the bowl.
neighbors.shared: a pause before eating turns hunger into gratitude.
neighbors.sources: Sabbasava Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: visit the graves
neighbors.text: Today Mexican families welcomed their dead home with photographs and marigolds. Muslims keep their dead close in their own way. The Prophet Muhammad, who had once forbidden visiting graves, later told people to visit them, for they remind you of the life to come. He also taught that when a person dies, a child who prays for them still brings them good.
neighbors.difference: Muslims visit graves and pray for the dead; Islamic teaching keeps graves simple, with no altars or offerings. Día de Muertos builds a welcoming table at home, held as loving tradition alongside the Church's prayers.
neighbors.shared: the people you've lost can still be prayed for.
neighbors.sources: Sahih Muslim, on visiting graves (paraphrase) · Sahih Muslim, three things that continue after death (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: continuing bonds
neighbors.text: Today the ofrenda kept faces from being forgotten. Grief researchers have noticed something similar. An older idea said healthy grieving meant letting go. Researchers writing about continuing bonds described mourners who keep a living connection to the person they lost: photos, rituals, talking to them, telling their stories. That bond, they found, can be part of healthy grief.
neighbors.difference: Continuing bonds describes what helps the living, without saying where the dead are. Catholics believe the dead are alive in God, and that the prayers of the living can still reach them.
neighbors.shared: love doesn't end where a life does.
neighbors.sources: Klass, Silverman & Nickman, Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief (1996) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: kirtan in the streets
neighbors.text: Today faith walked out the church door and down the street. Sikhs do this in nagar kirtan, a procession of hymns through the town. The Guru Granth Sahib rides in front on a decorated float, five Sikhs walk ahead in saffron robes, and the crowd sings while neighbors sweep the road and hand out food. In this age, Guru Arjan sings, kirtan is supreme.
neighbors.difference: On Corpus Christi, Catholics carry the Eucharist, which they believe is Christ himself. Sikhs carry the Guru Granth Sahib, honored as the living Guru in scripture; God, for Sikhs, is formless and never held in any object.
neighbors.shared: joy in the streets can be a kind of prayer.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1075 (Guru Arjan, Raag Maru) (paraphrase) · nagar kirtan in Sikh practice (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pulling the chariot
neighbors.text: Today the Eucharist passed over carpets of petals. In Puri, India, Hindus hold a festival procession called Rath Yatra. Jagannath, with his brother and sister, rides out of the temple on huge wooden chariots, and crowds pull them through the streets with ropes. Pulling the rope, devotees say, is itself a blessing.
neighbors.difference: Corpus Christi carries the Eucharist, which Catholics believe is Christ present under bread. At Rath Yatra, Hindus see Jagannath, a form of Krishna, coming out among the people in his sacred images.
neighbors.shared: holiness can leave the building and walk among the crowd.
neighbors.sources: Rath Yatra at the Jagannath temple, Puri (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: going forth
neighbors.text: Today the vows: poverty, chastity and obedience, lived together. Buddhism has its own monastic order. Monks and nuns go forth from home, shave their heads, own little beyond robes and a bowl, live celibate, and keep a shared code. The Buddha said household life is crowded and dusty, while going forth is like the open air.
neighbors.difference: Catholic vows are usually for life, made to God within the Church. In some Buddhist lands, people may ordain for a while and later return to lay life with honor; the aim is awakening, not union with a creator.
neighbors.shared: owning less can make room for what matters more.
neighbors.sources: Samaññaphala Sutta, Digha Nikaya 2 (paraphrase) · the Vinaya, the monastic code (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: brothers at Taizé
neighbors.text: Today a rich young man walked away sad, and religious life took up the invitation he couldn't. Some Protestant Christians took it up too. In Taizé, a French village, Brother Roger, a Swiss Protestant, founded a community of brothers, later joined by men from many churches. They commit for life to celibacy, to sharing all their goods, and to the guidance of the prior.
neighbors.difference: Catholic religious live under vows the Church recognizes, in communities the Church approves. Taizé is ecumenical, not a Catholic order. And many Protestant churches have no vowed communities, seeing marriage and work as the ordinary calling.
neighbors.shared: a shared table and a simple rule can hold a life.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:21 · Brother Roger, The Rule of Taizé (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when the rule runs out
neighbors.text: Today the Church's lawbook ended on its purpose, the salvation of souls, and asked for equity. Aristotle named equity long ago. Laws must speak in general terms, he wrote, so sometimes a rule misfires in a case its makers never pictured. Equity corrects the law there, doing what the lawgiver would have said had he been present.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle's equity serves justice in a city, judged by human reason. Canon law's equity serves a purpose beyond this life, the salvation of souls, and Catholics see Christ the shepherd behind every rule.
neighbors.shared: a rule is for people, and people are the point.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.10 (paraphrase) · Code of Canon Law, canon 1752

neighbors.heading: live by them
neighbors.text: Today canon law said the sheep are the point. Jewish law has its own top rule. Leviticus says of God's laws: "which if a man do, he shall live in them." The rabbis drew the lesson: live by them, not die by them. So saving a life overrides almost every commandment; if someone is in danger, you break Shabbat to help.
neighbors.difference: Canon law's highest rule looks to the salvation of souls, life with God beyond death. The rabbis' rule guards this life, the body in front of you, saved now, though Jewish law names a few acts never permitted, even to save a life.
neighbors.shared: the rules exist for people, never the other way around.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 18:5 (KJV) · Talmud, Yoma 85b (paraphrase) · Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one truth, many names
neighbors.text: Today the Church sent greetings for Diwali and said it rejects nothing true and holy in other religions. Hindus have an old line about the many ways people speak of the sacred. The Rig Veda says the wise call the one truth by many names. Some Hindus hear in it room for other religions, too, and welcome neighbors of every faith to share their feasts.
neighbors.difference: Nostra Aetate respects what is true and holy in other paths and, in the same breath, proclaims Christ as the way, the truth and the life. Some Hindus read the Rig Veda's line as many paths leading to one truth.
neighbors.shared: a greeting at your neighbor's feast is a small bridge.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 1.164.46 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: vie in good works
neighbors.text: Today the Church listened to other faiths before speaking. The Qur'an has its own words for living among them: "There is no compulsion in religion." And elsewhere: God gave each community its own law and way; had he willed, he could have made you one people. Instead he tests you in what he gave you, so race one another in good works.
neighbors.difference: The Church sees a ray of the truth in other religions while proclaiming Christ. Muslims hold the Qur'an as God's final message through Muhammad, and honor Jews and Christians as People of the Book, who received revelation before.
neighbors.shared: you can hold your faith firmly and still wish your neighbor well.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:256 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 5:48 (paraphrase)
